earlier_scan.source_named: Capell, Arthur (1976), phonology/text-doctype source for Onjob per Glottolog; otherwise only wordlists (Ray 1938, Strong 1911, MacDonnell 1915)

sources.citation: Rosetta Project (2010). Onjob Swadesh List (archive.org rosettaproject_onj_swadesh-1), no source stated.
sources.note: Plain 30-odd-item wordlist, no stress marks, no notes.

sources.citation: Hammarström's hh.bib (held Glottolog bibliography): entries tagged Onjob [onj].
sources.note: Only MacDonnell 1915 (1-page wordlist), Strong 1911 (wordlist), Ray 1938, Dutton 1971/1975/1982, Capell 1976, Lean 1986 (counting systems) carry the onj code; none is a phonology.

sources.citation: Barker, John. 2019. Mixed Grammars and Tangled Hierarchies: An Austronesian-Papuan Contact Zone in Papua New Guinea. Anthropological Forum 29(3): 284-301. doi:10.1080/00664677.2019.1624505. (Open copy on the WCAA 'Deja Lu' archive.)
sources.note: Nothing. Social anthropology of Collingwood Bay multilingualism (Maisin-centred); Onjob appears only for classification, location, oral history and the local Onjob/Aisor split; the words phonology/phonological occur only in the general discussion of Ross's metatypy and of Maisin; the one 'stress' token is 'I need to stress again' (p. 293). Searched the extracted text for stress, tone, tonal, accent, syllable, vowel, phonolog.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2018. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area: A Comprehensive Guide (The World of Linguistics 4), 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
sources.note: list entry only: 'Onjob [onj] 150; specific feature: Capell 1976'; the Dagan paragraph gives lexicostatistics and pronoun reconstructions; no prosody (the 'contrastive tone' sentence on the same page belongs to the preceding Chimbu-Wahgi section).

sources.citation: Carrington, Lois. 1996. A linguistic bibliography of the New Guinea area. Pacific Linguistics D-90. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU. xiii+476 pp. (language index s.v. Onjob (Onjab, Onjo); entries Chignell 1911, Dutton 1971/1973/1975, MacDonnell in Papua Annual Report 1914-15 'Airam (Onjob)', Stephens 1974, Strong 1911, Voegelin & Voegelin 1965, Wurm & Hattori 1981)
sources.note: No phonology content: it is a bibliography. Its value is negative evidence — the most complete New Guinea bibliography to 1995 knows no grammar, sketch, phonology or SIL manuscript for Onjob; only administrative vocabularies (1911, 1914-15), Dutton's surveys, a mission memoir (Chignell 1911) and an anthropology PhD on Wanigela kinship (Stephens 1974, U. North Carolina) with Onjob cultural notes.

sources.citation: Capell, A. (1976). Austronesian and Papuan 'Mixed' Languages: General Remarks. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol 2 (Pacific Linguistics C-39), pp. 527-579.
sources.note: Nothing about Onjob stress. Onjob appears only as the NAN contrast column in Table VI (pronouns, p. 558) and Table VIII (100-word list, pp. 563-568), plus two sentences saying it 'is NAN' (pp. 553, 558). The only 'stress' passages (pp. 573-574) concern Germanic/Finno-Ugric. This refutes the earlier scan's 'phonology/text-doctype' pointer.
sources.venue: New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol 2 (Pacific Linguistics C-39)

sources.citation: Dutton, T. E. (1975). South-Eastern Trans-New Guinea Phylum Languages. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38), pp. 613-664. Dagan sect. 2.9.5.6, pp. 640-641.
sources.note: Nothing. p. 640: 'None of the languages has been recorded or studied in any depth except Daga (or Dimuga).' Onjob paragraph (pp. 640-641) repeats the 1971 sociolinguistic note verbatim; no phonology.
sources.venue: New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study Vol 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-38)

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom (1971). Languages of South-East Papua. Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 14 (Pacific Linguistics A-28), pp. 1-46. Canberra: ANU. Dagan family pp. 16-18; sect. 4.31 Onjob p. 17.
sources.note: Nothing. Survey overview only: Onjob spoken in two villages (Koreaf, Naukwate); 'slight phonological differences between the two communalects'; lexicostatistics chart. No stress or accent statement anywhere in the volume for Onjob.
sources.venue: Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 14 (Pacific Linguistics A-28)

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page and reference table for onjo1240 (9 refs) and for the Dagan family daga1274 (112 refs).
sources.note: No descriptive (grammar/sketch/phonology) reference for Onjob; only Dutton 1971/1975, Capell 1976, Ray 1938, Strong 1911 and MacDonnell 1915 wordlists, Ethnologue, UNESCO Atlas, World Oral Literature Project. Family table adds nothing Onjob-specific beyond MacDonnell 1915.

sources.citation: Wikipedia 'Onjob language' and 'Dagan languages' articles (checked for references only).
sources.note: No phonology section; references are Ethnologue, a village-coordinates dataset, and a note that PARADISEC collections AC1 (Capell) and TD1 (Dutton) hold Onjob material (unpublished field recordings/notes).

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. (1938). The Languages of the Eastern and South-Eastern Divisions of Papua. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 68: 153-208 (Onjo/Dimuga group pp. 160-162).

sources.note: OLAC host could not be reached by automated download; SIL PNG and PARADISEC behind an automated-access block; Ethnologue and ElCat could not be reached by automated download. A partial held SIL OAI harvest (about 4,000 of the archive's records) has no onj record; the SIL OAI endpoint itself has no set hierarchy so an onj filter was impossible.
